process: Driver (prime mover) database, natural gas engine generator sets (Sect. 7.1, Tables 7.1-7.2, p.320-322)
description: Electric motor data (General Electric worksheets) in the OPGEE driver database.

process: Upgrader configuration: Delayed coking (Suncor-like), OSTUM-derived (Table 6.32, p.144-145)

process: Upgrader configuration: Hydroconversion plus fluid coking (Syncrude-like), OSTUM-derived (Table 6.32, p.144-145)
description: Integrated bitumen upgrader modelled with the Oil Sands Technology Upgrading Model (OSTUM) for Borealis Heavy Blend bitumen to a light sweet SCO (31.1 API, 0.11 wt% S): hydroconversion plus fluid coking (syncrude-like) with on-site hydrogen by steam methane reforming, process-gas and coke use, and cogeneration.

process: Upgrader configuration: Hydroconversion (Scotford-like), OSTUM-derived (Table 6.32, p.144-145)
description: Integrated bitumen upgrader modelled with the Oil Sands Technology Upgrading Model (OSTUM) for Borealis Heavy Blend bitumen to a light sweet SCO (31.1 API, 0.03 wt% S): hydroconversion (scotford-like) with on-site hydrogen by steam methane reforming, process-gas and coke use, and cogeneration.

process: Driver (prime mover) database, natural gas engine generator sets (Sect. 7.1, Tables 7.1-7.2, p.320-322)
description: Diesel engine data in the OPGEE driver database (energy consumption from gallons per hour).

process: Driver (prime mover) database, natural gas engine generator sets (Sect. 7.1, Tables 7.1-7.2, p.320-322)
description: Natural-gas internal combustion engine (Caterpillar data) and generator sets used by OPGEE to convert shaft or electric power demand into fuel use; energy consumption in Btu per bhp-hr.

process: Solar thermal steam generation for thermal EOR (Sect. 6.15.2.4, p.183)
description: Solar thermal (e.g. glasshouse trough) steam generation displacing part of the gas used to raise steam for thermal oil recovery.

process: Chlor-alkali electrolysis (EU-27 and EFTA plant data)
description: membrane cell chlor-alkali electrolysis (monopolar and bipolar), 40 EU plants

process: Oxygen-depolarised cathode (emerging technique)
description: membrane cells with oxygen-depolarised cathodes (reduce oxygen to hydroxide, no hydrogen co-product); commercialised by one manufacturer since June 2013

process: Anaerobic treatment (Sect. 3.3.2.3.5.2, Table 3.111)
description: Anaerobic treatment (contact, UASB, fixed-bed or expanded-bed reactor) converting the organic load in an airtight reactor to biogas of about 70 % methane and 30 % CO2, used as a high-load pretreatment ahead of aerobic treatment.

process: Evaporation (Sect. 3.3.2.3.4.15, Table 3.93)
description: Evaporation of waste water in evaporators operated in series (often under vacuum, 12-20 kPa and 50-60 degC), the condensation heat of one stage heating the preceding one; the concentrate is recycled or disposed of.

process: Activated sludge process, chemical-sector WWTPs (Sect. 3.3.3.1, Tables 3.130 and 3.133)
description: WWTP using the activated sludge process: equalisation, mixing/neutralisation station, primary clarifier, aeration basin or tower biology (optionally with nitrification/denitrification), final clarifier with sludge recycling, and sludge treatment.

process: Aerobic treatment (Sect. 3.3.2.3.5.4, Tables 3.117 and 3.121)
description: Complete mix activated sludge process: microorganisms kept in suspension in the waste water, the mixture mechanically aerated with air or pure oxygen, and the sludge separated (settling, flotation or membrane) and recycled to the aeration tank.

process: Aerobic treatment (Sect. 3.3.2.3.5.4, Tables 3.117 and 3.121)
description: Sequencing batch reactor: activated sludge treatment in a batch-operated tank (listed with the complete mix activated sludge process).

process: Flaring (Sect. 3.5.1.6, Table 3.298)
description: Elevated flare: high-temperature oxidation of combustible waste gas in an open flame at a stack tip, with pilot burners and steam or air assist; mainly a safety device for intermittent or emergency releases.

process: Catalytic oxidation (Sect. 3.5.1.3.6, Tables 3.208 and 3.211)
description: Recuperative catalytic oxidiser (catalytic oxidation of VOCs with recuperative preheating of the waste gas).

process: Catalytic oxidation (Sect. 3.5.1.3.6, Tables 3.208 and 3.211)
description: Regenerative catalytic oxidiser (catalytic oxidation of VOCs with regenerative preheating of the waste gas).

process: Catalytic oxidation (Sect. 3.5.1.3.6, Tables 3.208 and 3.211)
description: Straight catalytic oxidiser (catalytic oxidation of VOCs without flue-gas heat recovery).

process: Catalytic oxidation (Sect. 3.5.1.3.6, Tables 3.208 and 3.211)
description: Catalytic oxidiser: waste gas heated by auxiliary burners to about 300-500 degC then passed through a precious- or base-metal catalyst bed (fixed or fluidised), allowing oxidation at lower temperature than thermal oxidation.

process: Thermal oxidation (Sect. 3.5.1.3.5, Tables 3.202 and 3.206)
description: Recuperative thermal oxidiser: a combustion chamber with a waste gas preheater (and optionally a secondary heat exchanger) continuously transferring flue-gas heat; 50-80 % heat recovery, for 1 000-50 000 Nm3/h.

process: Thermal oxidation (Sect. 3.5.1.3.5, Tables 3.202 and 3.206)
description: Regenerative thermal oxidiser: the waste gas is preheated in a ceramic heat-exchange matrix, oxidised in a chamber held at 800-1 000 degC by burners, and leaves through a second matrix that stores its heat for the next cycle; 90-97 % heat recovery.

process: Central waste gas incineration, Plant 4 DE (Sect. 3.5.2, Table 3.299)
description: Two series combustion chambers (reduction at 1 350 degC, oxidation at 900 degC) for waste gases loaded with nitrogen oxides and organics; the heat raises 30-40 bar steam.

process: Central waste gas incineration, Plant 1 DE (Sect. 3.5.2, Table 3.299)
description: Central incinerator for organic waste gases from four installations at 850 degC (natural gas and methanol support fuel), followed by a two-stage wet scrubber.

process: Central waste gas incineration, Plant 2 DE (Sect. 3.5.2, Table 3.299)
description: Central incinerator for organic waste gases from four installations in a vertical chamber at >=850 degC (natural gas), followed by multi-stage scrubbing and an ionisation wet ESP for silica.

process: Central waste gas incineration, Plant 3 DE (Sect. 3.5.2, Table 3.299)
description: Central incinerator for organic waste gases above 900 degC (natural gas and liquid support fuels) with SNCR and a two-stage flue-gas scrubber.

process: Thermal oxidation (Sect. 3.5.1.3.5, Tables 3.202 and 3.206)
description: Straight thermal oxidiser: a combustion chamber heating the waste gas above the autoignition point of its contaminants with support fuel (e.g. natural gas), without heat recovery from the flue gas.

process: Wet air oxidation (Sect. 3.3.2.3.4.4.3, Table 3.63)
description: Wet air oxidation: refractory organics oxidised with air or oxygen in the liquid phase at elevated temperature and pressure (low-pressure 120-200 degC, 0.3-2 MPa; high-pressure up to 300 degC, 12 MPa), autothermal at about 6-8 g/l COD.

process: Aerobic treatment (Sect. 3.3.2.3.5.4, Tables 3.117 and 3.121)
description: Fixed-bed biofilter: biofilm held on a carrier (e.g. lignite coke) through which the waste water passes, backwashed regularly; a compact alternative to activated sludge without a secondary clarifier.

process: Aerobic treatment (Sect. 3.3.2.3.5.4, Tables 3.117 and 3.121)
description: Membrane bioreactor: suspended-growth activated sludge combined with microfiltration or ultrafiltration membranes (0.1-0.4 micron, submerged or in an external loop) that replace the secondary clarifier and tertiary filtration.

process: Membrane bioreactor, Roche Diagnostics Penzberg DE (Sect. 3.3.3.2)
description: Central biological WWTP: high-performance activated sludge stage with refined oxygen, then six aeration tanks in cascade, the last designed as a membrane bioreactor.

process: Membrane bioreactor, Sanofi-Chimie Aramon FR (Sect. 3.3.3.2, Table 3.137)
description: Two parallel membrane bioreactors (3 600 m3 each, retrofitted to conventional activated sludge in 2000) with high-rate, anoxic and low-rate zones treating pharmaceutical waste water (COD 3-30 g/l).

process: Stripping (Sect. 3.3.2.3.4.17, Tables 3.98 and 3.101)
description: Air stripping: volatile contaminants (solvents, ammonia, hydrogen sulphide) transferred from waste water to a counter-current air stream in a packed or tray column, with the stripping gas treated downstream.

process: Stripping (Sect. 3.3.2.3.4.17, Tables 3.98 and 3.101)
description: Steam stripping: volatile contaminants (ammonia, hydrogen sulphide, solvents) driven from waste water by live steam in a column, allowing recovery of the stripped substances.

process: Biomethane from anaerobic digestion with upgrading, Low/High cases (Sect. 3.2, Table 4)
description: Anaerobic digestion of wet organic feedstocks (35-60 degC, 1-50 day residence) to biogas, upgraded by CO2 and contaminant removal to 97% methane; typically 5-20 MW product output.
state-of-development: mature; about 500 upgrading plants in Europe in 2017

process: Corn fibre to cellulosic ethanol (D3MAX) at a 100 MGY (380,000 m3/yr) corn ethanol plant, 7.0 MGY (26,000 m3/yr) cellulosic ethanol (Sect. 3.3, Table 7)
description: Add-on to a corn dry-mill ethanol plant that converts the corn kernel fibre in the wet cake (acid treatment, enzymatic hydrolysis and fermentation in one tank, distillation, stillage drying) to cellulosic ethanol with zero feedstock cost and a higher-protein DDGS by-product credit.
state-of-development: first full-scale commercial plant (Ace Ethanol, Stanley, Wisconsin; 250 dry t/day wet cake, 14,000 m3/yr) under construction, start-up due October 2019

process: Corn fibre to cellulosic ethanol (D3MAX) at a 50 MGY (190,000 m3/yr) corn ethanol plant, 3.5 MGY (13,000 m3/yr) cellulosic ethanol (Sect. 3.3, Table 7)
description: Add-on to a corn dry-mill ethanol plant that converts the corn kernel fibre in the wet cake (acid treatment, enzymatic hydrolysis and fermentation in one tank, distillation, stillage drying) to cellulosic ethanol with zero feedstock cost and a higher-protein DDGS by-product credit.
state-of-development: first full-scale commercial plant (Ace Ethanol, Stanley, Wisconsin; 250 dry t/day wet cake, 14,000 m3/yr) under construction, start-up due October 2019

process: Ethanol from lignocellulosic sugar via fermentation, SGAB Low/Medium/High cases (Sect. 3.3, Table 6)
description: Pre-treatment, enzymatic hydrolysis and fermentation of lignocellulosic feedstocks (bagasse, straws, stover, wood residues) to ethanol, based on operating and commissioned projects in several regions.
state-of-development: commercial scale plants operating or commissioning (Raizen, Liberty, Crescentino, Kajaani) with several under construction (Table 5)

process: Biomass gasification to methanol or methane, SGAB Cost Report, Low/High, 200 MW (Sect. 3.4, Table 9)
description: Gasification of biomass to syngas, conditioning and synthesis to methanol or methane; E.ON (200 MW biomethane), VTT (200 MW methanol) and CHEMREC (100 MW methanol) projects scaled to 200 MW.
state-of-development: prospective; cost estimates mostly from engineering studies or plants under construction or commissioning, plant availability of 8000 hours not yet proven

process: Biomass gasification to methanol or methane, this work, Low/High, 200 MW (Sect. 3.4, Table 9)
description: Gasification of biomass to syngas, conditioning and synthesis to methanol or methane; updated with Enerkem, GoBiGas, GTI and other projects, many atmospheric gasifiers (25% higher specific investment than SGAB).
state-of-development: prospective; cost estimates mostly from engineering studies or plants under construction or commissioning, plant availability of 8000 hours not yet proven

process: Enerkem Edmonton, municipal solid waste (RDF) to ethanol (methanol), 30 MW (Sect. 3.4, SGAB)
description: Waste-to-methanol/ethanol plant in Edmonton, Canada using sorted municipal waste (RDF) as feedstock; output ethanol approximately 30 MW (38,000 m3/yr).

process: Waste (RDF) gasification to methanol or methane, this work, Low/High, 200 MW (Sect. 3.4, Table 9)
description: Gasification of waste-derived fuel (RDF) to syngas and synthesis to methanol or methane; feedstock cost -13 to 0 EUR/MWh (gate fee).
state-of-development: prospective; cost estimates mostly from engineering studies or plants under construction or commissioning, plant availability of 8000 hours not yet proven

process: Biomass gasification to Fischer-Tropsch liquids and gasoline, SGAB Cost Report, Low/High, 200 MW (Sect. 3.4, Table 10)
description: Biomass gasification, syngas conditioning, Fischer-Tropsch (or methanol/DME to gasoline) synthesis and upgrading; SGAB cost report based on a large number of studies, plant of about 200 MW.
state-of-development: prospective; cost estimates mostly from engineering studies or plants under construction or commissioning, plant availability of 8000 hours not yet proven

process: Biomass gasification to Fischer-Tropsch liquids and gasoline, this work, Low/High, 200 MW (Sect. 3.4, Table 10)
description: Biomass gasification, conditioning, Fischer-Tropsch synthesis and upgrading to liquid hydrocarbons; updated with KIT Bioliq, TIGAS (methanol/DME to gasoline), Red Rock, Fulcrum and others.
state-of-development: prospective; cost estimates mostly from engineering studies or plants under construction or commissioning, plant availability of 8000 hours not yet proven

process: Waste (RDF) gasification to Fischer-Tropsch liquids and gasoline, this work, Low/High, 200 MW (Sect. 3.4, Table 10)
description: Gasification of waste-derived fuel to Fischer-Tropsch liquids and gasoline; feedstock cost -12.5 to 0 EUR/MWh (gate fee).
state-of-development: prospective; cost estimates mostly from engineering studies or plants under construction or commissioning, plant availability of 8000 hours not yet proven

process: HVO, hydrotreated vegetable oil (refinery co-processing to stand-alone), Low/Medium/High cases (Sect. 3.1, Table 3)
description: Hydrotreating of vegetable oils and fats to hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO), covering refinery upgrade for co-processing, refinery revamps and stand-alone self-supporting plants.
state-of-development: mature; demand and capacity expanding rapidly

process: Pyrolysis oil, stand-alone upgrading, Low/High (Sect. 3.5, Table 11)
description: Fast pyrolysis of biomass and on-site hydrogenation to hydrocarbon fuel in a stand-alone plant.
state-of-development: prospective; co-processing explored in refinery pilot tests, integrated hydrogenation only at laboratory scale; cost data indicative from the SGAB report

process: Pyrolysis oil with refinery co-processing (FCC or hydrotreatment), Low/High (Sect. 3.5, Table 11)
description: Fast pyrolysis of biomass at about 500 degC and short residence time, recovery of pyrolysis oil, and upgrading by co-processing in a fossil refinery (blend-in limited to 2-10%).
state-of-development: prospective; co-processing explored in refinery pilot tests, integrated hydrogenation only at laboratory scale; cost data indicative from the SGAB report

process: Direct contact steam generation, NRCan HiPrOx (Sect. Steam Generation pp.20-21; Sect. GHG Emissions pp.60-62)
description: Steam produced by directly contacting water with hot flue gas from fuel burned with oxygen, no boiler tubes; the product gas (about 90% H2O, 10% CO2) is injected into the reservoir where part of the CO2 is expected to stay
state-of-development: pre-commercial; the study expects lengthy experimentation and piloting before it is commercially ready

process: OTSG as SAGD base-case steam generator (Sect. Study Approach, Steam Generation Technologies p.55)
OTSG at 78% steam quality, one generator (Sect. Steam Generation, Table 2.4 p.20)
description: Conventional oil-sands once-through steam generator (most industry OTSGs deliver about 78% steam quality) producing 101,887 kg/h of dry steam

process: SQ90 OTSG at 90% steam quality, one generator (Sect. Steam Generation, Table 2.4 p.20)
description: OTSG with rifled pipes in the radiant section (Innovative Steam Technologies) raising steam quality from about 78% to 90% without dry-out; commercially available

process: Gas-turbine once-through steam generator, ConocoPhillips/Total (Sect. Steam Generation p.24)
description: Turbine exhaust heat raises steam in an OTSG with a burner firing natural gas and part of the exhaust, producing electricity and SAGD steam; may not meet steam load if designed for power

process: Solid oxide fuel cell cogeneration for SAGD steam and power (Sect. Steam Generation pp.21-23)
description: Solid oxide fuel cell generating electricity electrochemically, with waste heat raising SAGD steam and the product stream injectable; fuel from methane reforming; operating temperature about 1,000 C

process: CCC bitumen-to-diesel configuration (Sect. CCC Process p.38)
description: Cold Catalytic Cracking configured to convert bitumen directly to diesel

process: Full upgrading benchmark: delayed coking upgrader, 30,000 bbl/d bitumen (Table 2.7 p.36; Tables A.3-A.4 p.95)
description: Delayed coking upgrader processing 30,000 bbl/d Athabasca bitumen to 26,500 bbl/d of 30-32 API SCO (diluent recovery, vacuum distillation, coker, naphtha and diesel hydrotreaters, mild hydrocracker, hydrogen and sulphur plants), the yardstick for partial upgrading technologies

process: Cold Catalytic Cracking (CCC) partial upgrading (Table 2.7 p.36; Sect. CCC Process pp.37-38)
description: Bayshore Petroleum process using a proprietary liquid catalyst at 400-450 C to convert bitumen to transport-ready partially upgraded product, without hydrogen or high pressure; gas, diesel and solid coke by-products

process: Desulphurization and Upgrading (DSU) (Table 2.7 p.36; Sect. DSU Process pp.38-39)
description: Field Upgrading sodium-metal process (about 350 C, 750 psig) that removes sulphur and metals from bitumen, heavy oil or vacuum residue with a small hydrogen input and electrolytic sodium recovery; product targeted at low-sulphur (0.1% S) bunker fuel
state-of-development: 10 bbl/d pilot; 2,500 bbl/d demonstration planned for 2019

process: Enhanced JetShear (EJS) partial upgrading, 30,000 bbl/d (Table 2.7 p.36; Sect. EJS Process pp.36-37)
description: Fractal Systems moderately high severity partial upgrading: pump and hammer-reactor system strips light ends and heats just below cracking temperature to cause cavitation and shearing, with olefin removal and low-pressure hydrogen polishing of the naphtha; product needs less diluent
state-of-development: between field and launch stages; 1,000 bbl/d commercial demonstration processed over 100,000 bbl in about one year (2015)

process: High Quality (Hi-Q) partial upgrading (Table 2.7 p.36; Sect. Hi-Q Process pp.40-41)
description: MEG Energy mild thermal cracking plus solvent de-asphalting giving asphalt-free, pipeline-ready heavy oil with overall yield up to 90%

process: Heavy to Light (HTL) partial upgrading (Table 2.7 p.36; Sect. HTL Process p.40)
description: Rapid high-temperature (about 500 C) pyrolysis in a circulating hot sand bed (Ivanhoe Energy, now FluidOil) giving pipeline-ready product without diluent; can burn lighter products to run as a net zero natural gas importer
state-of-development: demonstration phase; economic at 10,000-150,000 bbl/d feed

process: Increased Yields and Qualities (IYQ) upgrading (Table 2.7 p.36; Sect. IYQ Process pp.39-40)
description: ETX Systems primary upgrading in a cross-flow fluidized bed reactor (fluidized by recycle or natural gas) that vaporizes bitumen into VGO, diesel and kerosene cuts for deep conversion, 0.89 bbl distillable liquids per bbl against about 0.80 for delayed coking, no diluent needed

process: Electromagnetic heating with solvent, ESEIEH (Table 2.6 p.27; Sect. ESEIEH Process pp.31-32)
description: Enhanced solvent extraction incorporating electromagnetic heating: horizontal well pairs with a radio-frequency antenna heating connate water, plus propane or butane solvent to cut viscosity (Harris, CNOOC, Devon, Suncor)
state-of-development: demonstration project (CCEMC ranking); pilot at Suncor/Harris Dover facility

process: Electromagnetic heating, RF XL process (Sect. RF XL Process pp.32-33)
description: Radio-frequency heating of the connate water by a down-hole antenna (Acceleware with General Electric), alone or with solvent or gas injection; cost characteristics similar to ESEIEH

process: SEGD, in situ thermal extraction by down-hole oxy-combustion (Table 2.6 p.27; Sect. SEGD Process p.34)
description: Steam Environmental Generated Drainage (Valence Energy): natural gas burned with oxygen in a horizontal well generates steam sub-surface from injected water; steam and flue gas heat the reservoir by gravity drainage

process: SAGD base case, 30,000 bbl/d (Table 2.6 p.27; Sect. Study Approach pp.51-54; Tables A.1-A.2 pp.93-94)
description: Conventional SAGD benchmark modelled on the PTAC 2012 base case: Athabasca oil-rich reservoir, natural-gas OTSGs at 80% efficiency injecting 100% quality steam, electric submersible pumps, free-water knock-out and treaters, warm lime softening; produces bitumen for dilbit

process: Steam-surfactant process, Cenovus/Suncor (Table 2.6 p.27; Sect. Steam-Surfactant Process pp.33-34)
description: SAGD with surfactants (petroleum sulfonates, 0.01-0.1% of injected fluid) added to steam to lower interfacial tension and raise recovery; piloted by Suncor on three well pairs at MacKay River in 2013, continuing on three full pads

process: Steam-solvent processes SAP and SA-SAGD, generic (Table 2.6 p.27; Sect. Steam-Solvent Processes pp.29-31)
description: Steam co-injected with hydrocarbon solvent (butane, propane, condensate) in SAGD wells, cutting steam-oil ratio and raising bitumen production; at least nine SAGD operations have tested or implemented it

process: SA-SAGD, Solvent-Assisted SAGD, Imperial Cold Lake (Sect. SA-SAGD Process pp.30-31)
description: Imperial Oil process injecting up to 20 vol% hydrocarbon solvent with 80 vol% dry steam in a dual horizontal well configuration; pilot at Cold Lake Clearwater formation
state-of-development: ready for full-scale commercial application; proposed for Imperial Cold Lake Expansion

process: Narrows Lake SAP project, proposed (Sect. SAP Process p.30)
SAP, Solvent Aided Process, Senlac pilot (Sect. SAP Process pp.29-30)
description: Cenovus solvent-aided process: a small amount of hydrocarbon solvent (about 10 wt% of the steam injection rate) added to SAGD steam; solvent recovery above 70%

process: Pure solvent extraction, Nsolv process (Table 2.6 p.27; Sect. Pure Solvent Processes pp.28-29)
description: Heated condensing solvent (propane or butane vapour, 40-60 C, near reservoir pressure) replaces steam: it condenses, dissolves bitumen and leaves asphaltenes and metals in situ; solvent purified and re-injected; partially upgraded 13-14 API product

process: Tissue mill steam supply to the Yankee, about 5 t/h paper (Sect. 2.1-3.1, Tables 1-3, 7, 11)

process: Tissue mill steam supply to the Yankee, about 5 t/h paper (Sect. 2.1-3.1, Tables 1-3, 7, 11)

process: Tissue machine drying section, Layout 1 natural gas (Sect. 2.1.1, Table 1)
description: State-of-the-art tissue drying section with high heat recovery: a single steam-heated Yankee cylinder (9 bar) plus hot-air impingement hoods fired with natural gas (air up to 500 degC); the sheet enters at 45% (printed as diluted at 45% mass based in water; consistent with 45% solids given 5.5 t/h evaporation) and leaves at 5% moisture.

process: HTHP specific investment costs cited from the literature (Sects. 1.3, 3.3)

process: Additional mass balances for selected pathways (Table 13.4-1)

description: E-fuel plant (electrolysis, CO2 capture, RWGS, FT) whose e-wax is co-fed (5%, 30%) or fully fed (100%) to the refinery hydrocracker.

process: Mass balance for example pathways (Table 6.2.9-1)

state-of-development: Refinery co-processing trials problematic; additional R&D required; small commercial pyrolysis plants 20-50 kt/a.

process: Specific investment for example pathways (Table 6.2.9-2)
description: New refinery stabilisation hydrotreater plus hydrocracker adaptation for purchased raw pyrolysis/HTL oil.

process: Dedicated lipid hydrotreatment, ~1 Mt/a plants (Sect. 5.2.2)

state-of-development: Commercial (stand-alone operations up to 1 Mt/a; dedicated EU capacity ~2-3 Mt/a).

process: Mass balance for example pathways (Table 6.2.9-1)
description: Lipid hydrotreatment (Lipid to HDT) as modelled in RafXl.

process: Specific investment for example pathways (Table 6.2.9-2)

process: Lipid co-processing in existing diesel hydrotreater (Sect. 5.2.3, Table 5.2.4-1)

state-of-development: Commercial at 5-10% co-feed; up to 30% achieved commercially under special circumstances (Topsoe).

process: Specific investment for example pathways (Table 6.2.9-2)
description: Co-processing of lipids with fossil gas-oil in an existing refinery hydrotreater (or hydrocracker).

process: Hydrocracker transformation to 100% lipid feed (Sect. 5.2.2, Table 5.2.4-1)

state-of-development: Done or announced at three European refineries (ENI 2015, Total 2015).

process: Specific investment for example pathways (Table 6.2.9-2)

process: Noranda-Teniente with dry feed + slag flotation, concentrate to anode (Table V)

process: Noranda reactor (filter cake) + Peirce-Smith converters + slag flotation, concentrate to anode (Table III, V)
description: Noranda reactor: horizontal bath smelting vessel with side tuyeres, wet concentrate top-fed, limited to about 45% oxygen enrichment; matte converted in Peirce-Smith converters and slag cleaned by milling and flotation.

process: Bottom blowing smelting (SKS/BBS, filter cake) + Peirce-Smith converters + slag flotation, concentrate to anode (Table IV, V)
description: Bottom blowing smelting (SKS/BBS): cylindrical bath vessel with bottom shrouded oxygen injectors at 50-75% oxygen enrichment and top feeding of wet concentrate; Dongying reference plant; matte converted in Peirce-Smith converters.

process: Mitsubishi Process, concentrate to anode (Table V)
description: Mitsubishi continuous smelting-converting process (Coursol et al. 2010 comparison).

process: Flash smelting-flash converting-slag flotation, concentrate to anode (Table V)
description: Oxygen-enriched flash smelting with flash converting and slag flotation (Coursol et al. 2010 comparison).

process: KH hot-calcine reverberatory furnace route, concentrate to anode (Table V)
description: Reverberatory furnace smelting of hot calcine (Kellogg and Henderson 1976 benchmark; the older practice the modern vessels replaced).

process: Isasmelt-Peirce-Smith converting-rotary slag cleaning, concentrate to anode (Table V)
description: Isasmelt top-submerged-lance smelting with Peirce-Smith converting and rotary slag cleaning (Coursol et al. 2010 comparison).

process: TP 38 Alkali-activated binders
description: Two-component binder of a reactive alumosilicate (metakaolin, fly ash, GBFS) and an alkaline activator forming a geopolymer network.
state-of-development: Demonstration; first industrial plant built in Australia; non-structural uses only.

process: TP 34 Clinker reduction by fly ash
description: Cement with 25 to 35 mass% coal fly ash replacing clinker.

process: TP 31 Clinker reduction by GBFS
description: Cement with 30 to 70 mass% granulated blast furnace slag replacing clinker.

process: TP 37 Clinker reduction by limestone
description: Cement with 25 to 35 mass% limestone (other materials: silica fume, burnt shale) replacing clinker.

process: TP 35 Clinker reduction by natural pozzolanas
description: Cement with 15 to 35 mass% natural pozzolana replacing clinker.

process: TP 29 Optimised particle size distribution
description: Separate grinding and blending to an optimised cement particle size distribution, allowing up to 5% more limestone or slag.

process: TP 36 Clinker reduction by calcined pozzolanas
description: Cement with 15 to 35 mass% calcined clay (natural calcined pozzolana), without limestone.

process: TP 36 Clinker reduction by calcined pozzolanas
description: Cement with up to 35 mass% calcined clay combined with up to 15 mass% limestone (LC3-type).

process: TP 39 Cements based on carbonation of calcium silicates
description: Low-lime calcium silicate clinker (wollastonite/rankinite, e.g. Solidia) burnt at about 1200 degC in rotary kilns and hardened by CO2 curing.
state-of-development: First industrial trials in rotary kilns; commercial launch planned for precast elements.

process: TP 40 Pre-hydrated calcium silicates
description: Celitement: lime calcination, autoclave synthesis of alpha-C2SH at about 200 degC and 12 bar, then activation inter-grinding with quartz.
state-of-development: R&D; first industrial-scale plant planned for 2017/2018.

process: TP 42 Belite calcium sulfoaluminate clinker
description: Belite calcium sulfoaluminate (BCSA) clinker burnt in conventional kilns at 150-200 degC lower sintering temperature, easier to grind.

process: TP 6 Mono-channel to multi-channel burner
description: Replacing a mono-channel burner (20-25% primary air) by a modern multi-channel burner (8-12%), so more hot secondary air from the cooler is used.

process: TP 46 Calcium looping
description: Tail-end calcium looping: CaO carbonator (600-700 degC) and oxy-fired calciner (>900 degC) fluidised beds; purge used as raw material; integrated variant replaces the precalciner.
state-of-development: Lab and pilot scale; Taiwan Cement/ITRI pilot since 2013 capturing 1 t CO2/h.

process: TP 45 Post-combustion capture by membranes
description: Gas separation or gas absorption membranes on cement kiln flue gas, with CO2 purification and compression to 80 bar.
state-of-development: Research scale; about 10 years needed to reach industrial application.

process: TP 47 Mineral carbonation
description: Capture and storage by reacting Mg/Ca silicates (serpentine, olivine, wollastonite) or industrial wastes with CO2 to stable carbonates.
state-of-development: R&D phase; no large-scale units for flue gas.

process: TP 8 Efficient clinker cooler
description: Optimising an existing 2nd-generation grate cooler (new grate plates, static inlet grate, modified aeration).

process: TP 8 Efficient clinker cooler
description: Conversion from a planetary cooler to a newest-generation reciprocating grate cooler (heat recuperation up to 75-80%, heat loss <0.42 MJ/kg cli) at 6,000 t/d.

process: TP 20 Auxiliary system efficiency
description: Optimising compressed air and lighting, and replacing IE1 by IE3 motors.

process: TP 15 Pre-treatment of alternative fuel
description: Drying (belt, drum, flash dryers with cooler vent air) and grinding of alternative fuels such as sewage sludge or RDF before kiln firing.

process: TP 16 Gasification or pre-combustion of alternative fuels
description: Pre-combustion chamber or gasifier (fixed bed, fluidised bed above 10 MW) supplying lean gas (4-6 MJ/m3 with air) from alternative fuels to the calciner.

process: TP 25 Optimisation of ball mill operating parameters
description: Optimising ball charge, filling, liners, walls and separator settings of existing ball mills.

process: TP 28 Separate grinding and blending by fineness
description: Coarse fraction on VRM/HPGR plus a fine-grinding device (e.g. stirred media mill), blended.

process: TP 22 Plant operation with renewable power
description: Oversized mills and silos allowing flexible grinding when surplus renewable power is available.

process: TP 26 Separate grinding of raw material components
description: Grinding hard raw material components (sand, slag) separately from the main raw mix.

process: TP 23 VRM and roller presses for cement grinding
description: Vertical roller mills or high pressure grinding rolls (alone or with a ball mill) for raw and cement grinding; specific energy about 70% (VRM) or 50% (HPGR) of a ball mill.

process: TP 5 Increase of kiln capacity
description: New 6,000 t/d BAT kiln line replacing smaller (e.g. two 3,000 t/d) kilns; specific heat losses fall with plant size.

process: TP 14 Alternative fuels incl. biomass
description: Raising the substitution of fossil fuels by waste and biomass fuels to up to 65% of kiln fuel energy (may raise specific energy demand up to 8.5%).

process: TP 41 Belite cements
description: Belite clinker (LSF 78-85) burnt at about 1350 degC in conventional kilns, with up to 90% belite.

process: TP 44 Post-combustion capture by absorption
description: Post-combustion chemical absorption (MEA or advanced amines; chilled ammonia in development) on cement kiln flue gas, with regeneration steam at 350-450 kPa and CO2 compression.
state-of-development: Pilot: Aker mobile test unit at Brevik (Norway) 2013-2016, about 8,000 h, 2,000 t CO2/yr; SkyMine (San Antonio) NaOH-based capture up to 75,000 t CO2/yr.

process: TP 2 Change from long kilns to preheater/precalciner kilns
description: Retrofit converting a long wet or long dry kiln to a multi-stage cyclone preheater with precalciner and modern cooler.

process: TP 12 Alternative de-carbonated raw materials
description: Replacing part of the raw meal (10-15%) with de-carbonated calcium-bearing materials such as granulated blast furnace slag.

process: TP 13 Fuel switching (coal to oil or gas)
description: Switching kiln fuel from hard coal to oil or natural gas (40% lower CO2 per energy for gas, 16% for oil).

process: Thermal efficiency state of the art (SOTA Paper 1)
description: Dry-process kilns with precalcining technology, GNR weighted average of specific thermal energy demand (2014).

process: TP 33 Very high/very low lime saturation factor
description: Clinker with lime saturation factor lowered by 10 units, less CaCO3 and lower burning temperature.

process: TP 7 Oxygen enrichment
description: Oxygen-enriched combustion air (cryogenic ASU) raising flame temperature, reducing fuel demand by up to 5% and raising capacity.

process: Reference plant (Annex II)
description: Reference dry-process cement plant at 0.5 Mio. t/a clinker annual capacity (investment cost case of Annex II).

process: Reference plant (Annex II)
description: Reference dry-process cement plant at 1 Mio. t/a clinker annual capacity (investment cost case of Annex II).

process: Reference plant (Annex II)
description: Reference state-of-the-art dry-process kiln with preheater and precalciner (GNR-2014 world-average based reference plant), 6,000 t clinker/d, used as the basis for all technology-paper calculations.

process: Thermal efficiency state of the art (SOTA Paper 1)
description: State-of-the-art dry preheater cement kiln with 3 cyclone stages: range of average yearly fuel energy requirement from the Research Institute of the Cement Industry (Germany) study for the European BAT process.

process: Thermal efficiency state of the art (SOTA Paper 1)
description: State-of-the-art dry preheater cement kiln with 4 cyclone stages: range of average yearly fuel energy requirement from the Research Institute of the Cement Industry (Germany) study for the European BAT process.

process: Thermal efficiency state of the art (SOTA Paper 1)
description: State-of-the-art dry preheater cement kiln with 5 cyclone stages: range of average yearly fuel energy requirement from the Research Institute of the Cement Industry (Germany) study for the European BAT process.

process: Thermal efficiency state of the art (SOTA Paper 1)
description: State-of-the-art dry preheater cement kiln with 6 cyclone stages: range of average yearly fuel energy requirement from the Research Institute of the Cement Industry (Germany) study for the European BAT process.

description: Spray casting: liquid metal atomised and droplets deposited on a substrate (5-20 mm); low yield; early development, more likely for specialty products.

description: Strip casting: liquid steel cast directly on a belt or rolls to 1-10 mm; hot rolling and reheating are eliminated; no commercial strip casters yet.
state-of-development: Demonstration/pilot plant: more than 30 R&D projects, at least six at demonstration stage (ladle above 10 t); no commercial strip caster yet.

description: Coke oven of the reference ironmaking route with its direct investment cost per t of hot metal.

description: Modern electric arc furnace melting a 100% scrap charge.

process: Scrap-based steelmaking, Table 12 (Sect. 6.3) - K-ES process (100% scrap)
description: Klockner electric steelmaking: EAF with bottom inert gas stirring and coal/coke injection (22-30 kg/tcs) replacing part of the electricity; three companies operated it in 1993.
state-of-development: Commercial/demonstration: operated by three companies in 1993.

process: Finger shaft furnace with hot metal, Cockerill Sambre (Sect. 6.3)

process: Scrap-based steelmaking, Table 12 (Sect. 6.3) - Combination shaft furnace (100% scrap, design value)
description: Combination shaft furnace (VAI/Fuchs): rotating scrap preheating shaft (to about 1000 degC) alternating between two furnaces; design values stated by the developer.

process: Scrap-based steelmaking, Table 12 (Sect. 6.3) - HYLSA finger shaft furnace (55% DRI, 45% scrap)
description: DC finger shaft furnace at HYLSA (Mexico) charging 55% DRI and 45% scrap; DRI cannot be preheated and carries slag to melt.

process: Scrap-based steelmaking, Table 12 (Sect. 6.3) - Von Roll finger shaft furnace (100% scrap)
description: Finger shaft EAF (VAI/Fuchs) preheating scrap in a shaft above the furnace with process gas; operating at Von Roll/SWG, Switzerland.
state-of-development: Commercial: operating furnace (single finger shaft furnace is the most efficient 100%-scrap EAF in operation).

process: Scrap-based steelmaking, Table 12 (Sect. 6.3) - KS process (100% scrap, fossil fuel only)
description: Klockner steelmaking: scrap melted in a converter with bottom coal injection, oxygen and postcombustion, no electricity.

process: Scrap-based steelmaking, Table 12 (Sect. 6.3) - KVA process (100% scrap, fossil fuel only)
description: Klockner Voest Alpine: continuous scrap melting with oxygen and natural gas burners and postcombustion; refining in a separate reactor; R&D stopped.
state-of-development: Concept: R&D stopped (environmental problems, high scrap price).

process: Near-net-shape casting (Sect. 6.2, Tables 10-11) - thin slab casting (inline strip production)
description: Thin slab casting: slabs of 40-90 mm cast and rolled in line; commercial since 1985, mostly with EAFs; the inline strip production variant heats with an induction furnace so no fuel is needed.
state-of-development: Commercial (about 15 thin slab casters installed or ordered worldwide by 1995; about 10% of world hot strip).

process: Thin slab caster planned at Hoogovens (Sect. 6.2)
description: Thin slab caster to be installed at Hoogovens, annual capacity 1.2 million t strip/yr.

process: Thin slab caster planned at Thyssen (Sect. 6.2)
description: Thin slab caster to be installed at Thyssen, annual capacity 1.5 million t strip/yr.

process: Near-net-shape casting (Sect. 6.2, Tables 10-11) - thin slab casting with liquid core reduction (CPR)
description: Casting pressing rolling: slab squeezed with a liquid core after the mould to 10-25 mm; still needs a reheating furnace and rolling mill.
state-of-development: Commercial/demonstration: pilot plant in Germany since 1993.

process: Arex direct reduction plant, alternative source (Sect. 6.4)
description: Arex plant with the energy requirement reported as a single total per t DRI by an alternative source (ref. 94).

process: Arex direct reduction plant (Sect. 6.4)
description: Arex (Midrex improvement): hot DRI in the shaft acts as catalyst so gas reforming and ore reduction occur in the same reactor, lowering investment and SEC; gas-based shaft DR, the most efficient commercial DR process.
state-of-development: Commercial (applied in Venezuela); Midrex process produces 65% of world DRI.

process: Reference route investment, sinter plant component (Table 9)
description: Sinter plant of the reference ironmaking route with its direct investment cost per t of hot metal.

process: AISI direct steel-making process (Sect. 6.1, Table 8)
description: AISI process: partially prereduced pellets melted in foaming slag above an iron bath, coal top-fed, oxygen lanced, postcombustion about 40%.
state-of-development: Pilot: 15 t/day pilot plant; 350 kt/yr demonstration plant never built; development of direct iron making from ore stalled (1998).

process: CCF smelting reduction (Sect. 6.1, Table 8)
description: Cyclone converter furnace (Hoogovens): melting and prereduction cyclone mounted on a converter-type vessel; coal and oxygen lanced into the bath, postcombustion in the bath and cyclone.
state-of-development: Pilot: 20 t/h melting-cyclone test facility (1994); converter not tested at pilot scale; 700 kt/yr demonstration plant planned for 2000 with Dutch government support.

process: COREX smelting reduction (Sect. 6.1, Table 8)
description: COREX: coal gasified in a fluidised bed in the dome of the melter-gasifier, ore prereduced 90-95% in a shaft; the only commercial smelting reduction process, with high-calorific export gas (7.5 MJ/Nm3) and no postcombustion.
state-of-development: Commercial: C-1000 plant (300 kt/yr) in South Africa since 1989; C-2000 plant in Korea since 1995; further C-2000 orders placed (1998).

process: DIOS smelting reduction (Sect. 6.1, Table 8)
description: DIOS: three stacked fluidised-bed vessels (preheating, prereduction 25%, smelting reduction vessel with three-layer bath), oxygen lance, postcombustion 40-60%.
state-of-development: Pilot: 180 kt/yr pilot 1993-1995 (Japan); first commercial unit aimed for 2000, process available 2010-2015 at the latest.

process: HIsmelt smelting reduction (Sect. 6.1, Table 8)
description: HIsmelt: horizontal vessel with bottom-injected non-coking coal, hot blast instead of oxygen and fluidised-bed prereduction; postcombustion above 60% in the pilot plant.
state-of-development: Pilot: 100 kt/yr pilot plant at Kwinana (Australia) since 1994; first commercial plant (500-1000 kt/yr) planned for 1999.

process: Jupiter smelting reduction (Sect. 6.1, Table 8)
description: Jupiter (IRSID): process developed to supply virgin metal to EAF plants; R&D appears to have stopped.
state-of-development: Never tested at pilot-plant scale; R&D seems to have stopped (1998). No cost figures available.

process: Romelt smelting reduction (Sect. 6.1, Table 8)
description: Romelt: single-stage process with coal and ore fed to a large horizontal vessel, two-level side tuyeres, postcombustion about 70%, reduction in a foamy slag layer.
state-of-development: Pilot: 18 t/h pilot plant 1985-1988; 1000 kt/yr demonstration plant approved but never realised; licences to ICF Kaiser and Nippon Steel (1995).

description: MVR displacing fossil-fired steam with renewable electricity; also reduces water losses (about 5.2 GL/year if adopted by all Australian refineries).

description: Mechanical vapour recompression applied to high-temperature digestion; may need coupling with electric boilers.

process: MVR, low-temperature refineries (Table 4.1, p.22)
description: Mechanical vapour recompression: recompresses waste vapour with electricity to give Bayer process steam, recovering heat otherwise lost; needs about one third of the power of an electric boiler; not yet proven for alumina refining.

process: Concentrated solar thermal in alumina refining (Sect. 4.7.4, p.29)
description: CST can raise steam directly or store heat for overnight steam; under study for digestion steam, solar reforming and direct solar calcining; needs excellent solar resource, land and has high capex.

Atmospheric distillation, U.S. 1996 (Table 3-1)
description: Crude oil, after desalting, is heated in a fired heater and separated in an atmospheric column into gases, naphtha, kerosene, distillates and atmospheric residue; desalting energy included.

process: Vacuum distillation, U.S. 1996 (Table 3-2)
description: Atmospheric residue is reheated and fractionated under vacuum into gas oils and vacuum residue.

process: Lubricating oil manufacture, U.S. 1996 (Table 9-1)
description: Lube base stocks are made from vacuum distillates and residue by solvent deasphalting, solvent dewaxing and solvent extraction, with single-effect evaporative solvent recovery.

process: Claus sulfur recovery (Table 10-1)
description: Hydrogen sulfide from amine treating and sour water stripping is partly burnt to SO2 and reacted over a catalyst to elemental sulfur (Claus process), recovery assumed 99.7%.

process: Hydrofluoric acid alkylation, U.S. 1996 (Table 6-2)
description: Isobutane is combined with light olefins over hydrofluoric acid catalyst, with acid regeneration by distillation, to make alkylate.

process: Sulfuric acid alkylation, U.S. 1996 (Table 6-1)
description: Isobutane is combined with light olefins over sulfuric acid catalyst, with refrigeration to hold the low reaction temperature, to make alkylate.

process: Catalytic reforming, U.S. 1996 (Table 5-1)
description: Naphtha is converted over a platinum catalyst in a series of fired-heater/reactor stages to high-octane reformate, producing hydrogen as a by-product.

process: Delayed coking, U.S. 1996 (Table 4-5)
description: Heavy residue is heated in a furnace and held in coke drums where it cracks to gas, naphtha and gas oils and leaves petroleum coke.

process: Ethers manufacture, U.S. 1996 (Table 8-1)
description: Isobutylene or isoamylenes are reacted with methanol or ethanol over an acid resin catalyst to make MTBE, ETBE or TAME oxygenates.

process: Fluid coking and Flexicoking, U.S. 1996 (Table 4-6)
description: Fluid coking with an added gasifier that converts most of the coke to a low-Btu fuel gas (20-40 Btu/scf).

process: Fluid catalytic cracking, U.S. 1996 (Table 4-7)
description: Gas oil is cracked over a circulating fluidized catalyst; coke deposited on the catalyst is burnt off in the regenerator, whose heat drives the reaction and raises steam.

process: Fluid coking and Flexicoking, U.S. 1996 (Table 4-6)
description: Residue is sprayed onto a fluidized bed of hot coke particles where it cracks; part of the coke is burnt in a burner vessel to supply the heat.

process: Catalytic hydrocracking, U.S. 1996 (Table 4-8)
description: Heavy gas oils are cracked over a catalyst in a hydrogen-rich atmosphere at high pressure, giving lighter, low-sulphur products.

process: Catalytic hydrotreating, U.S. 1996 (Table 7-1)
description: Petroleum fractions are heated with hydrogen and passed over a fixed catalyst bed to remove sulfur, nitrogen and metals and saturate olefins.

process: Isobutane manufacture, U.S. 1996 (Table 8-2)
description: Normal butane is isomerized to isobutane over a catalyst in a hydrogen atmosphere (UOP Butamer).

process: Isobutylene manufacture (Table 8-4)
description: Skeletal isomerization of n-butenes to isobutylene for ether feed (CDTECH ISOMPLUS).

process: Isopentane and isohexane manufacture, U.S. 1996 (Table 8-3)
description: Light straight-run naphtha (pentanes and hexanes) is isomerized to branched isomers to raise octane.

process: Visbreaking, U.S. 1996 (Table 4-4)
description: Mild thermal cracking of residue in a furnace coil or soaker drum to reduce viscosity; capacity-weighted mix of 33% coil and 67% soaker units.

process: EAF steelmaking energy use, U.S. 1998 (Table 5-1, p.63)

process: Ammonium nitrate manufacture, U.S. 1997 (Table 5-6)
description: Ammonia neutralized with nitric acid, the solution concentrated and solidified by prilling or granulation, then cooled, screened and coated

process: Ammonium phosphate manufacture, U.S. 1997 (Table 5-11)

process: Ammonium sulfate manufacture, U.S. 1997 (Table 5-7)

process: Phosphoric acid manufacture, wet process, U.S. 1997 (Table 5-9)

process: Sulfuric acid manufacture, U.S. 1997 (Table 5-8)
description: Contact process: elemental sulfur burned with dry air, SO2 converted to SO3 over vanadium catalyst and absorbed in sulfuric acid; heat recovered as export steam and power

process: Superphosphate manufacture, U.S. 1997 (Table 5-12)
description: Ground phosphate rock reacted with sulfuric acid (normal) or phosphoric acid (triple superphosphate), cured, granulated and dried

process: Urea manufacture, U.S. 1997 (Table 5-4)

process: Ammonia manufacture, U.S. 1997 (Table 5-3)
description: Natural gas (or other hydrocarbon) desulfurized, steam reformed over nickel catalyst, shifted, CO2 removed and methanated, then synthesized to ammonia at high pressure over iron catalyst

process: Install electric compressors (PRO 103)

process: Recover gas from pipeline pigging operations (PRO 505)

process: Wet seal degassing recovery system (PRO 2014): one centrifugal compressor

process: Wet seal degassing recovery system (PRO 2014): station with four centrifugal compressors
description: High-pressure seal-oil/gas disengagement separators on each seal with demister/filter, routing gas entrained in wet-seal oil to compressor suction, turbine fuel, heater fuel or flare instead of venting it at the degassing tank.

process: Redesign blowdown systems and alter ESD practices (PRO 908): install YALE closures for ESD testing
description: Fit screwed-on YALE closure caps with bleed needle valves to ESD valve vent stacks so each ESD valve can be tested individually instead of an annual total station dump.

process: Replace gas starters with air or nitrogen (PRO 101): compressed air
description: Fill the engine starter volume tank with compressed air instead of natural gas, so starter turbine exhaust and volume tank leakage contain no methane.

process: Replace gas starters with air or nitrogen (PRO 101): nitrogen
description: Fill the engine starter volume tank with compressed nitrogen instead of natural gas, so starter turbine exhaust and volume tank leakage contain no methane.

process: Install electric motor starters (PRO 105)
description: Replace the gas expansion turbine starter on a compressor engine with an electric motor starter, removing starter gas venting and volume tank leakage.

process: Install electronic flare ignition devices (PRO 903): A, no on-site power
description: Replace a continuously burning flare pilot with an electronic sparking ignition device (battery with solar recharge at remote sites), optionally with pilot flame sensors.

process: Install electronic flare ignition devices (PRO 903): B, on-site power available
description: Replace a continuously burning flare pilot with an electronic sparking ignition device (battery with solar recharge at remote sites), optionally with pilot flame sensors.

process: Install flares (PRO 904)

process: Portable desiccant dehydrators (PRO 207)

process: Pipe glycol dehydrator to vapor recovery unit (PRO 203)

process: Reroute glycol skimmer gas (PRO 201)

process: Zero emissions dehydrators (PRO 206)

process: Inspect flowlines annually (PRO 404)

process: Conduct DI&M at remote sites (PRO 901)

process: Increase walking survey from a 5- to 3-year basis (PRO 902)

process: Insert gas main flexible liners (PRO 402)

process: Convert water tank blanket from natural gas to produced CO2 gas (PRO 503)

process: Install excess flow valves (PRO 603)
description: Install excess flow valves on new and replacement high-pressure distribution service lines; the valve snaps shut when a line is severed and stops the release.

process: Nitrogen rejection unit optimization (PRO 905): monitoring, maintenance and process optimization
description: Add a continuous-monitoring gas chromatograph on the NRU reject stream, clean exchangers and tune pressures and temperatures of the cryogenic nitrogen rejection unit to cut the methane vented with the rejected nitrogen.

process: Nitrogen rejection unit optimization (PRO 905): optimization plus Phase I tray upgrades

process: Install pressurized storage of condensate (PRO 501)
description: Store condensate and interstage knockout liquids in pressurized tanks and move them in pressurized transport to a gas plant, so the methane dissolved at pipeline pressure does not flash and vent from atmospheric tanks.

process: Replace burst plates with secondary relief valves (PRO 605)
description: Install a pressure relief valve on top of a rupture disc (burst plate), so after a rupture the valve recloses once pressure falls instead of venting until the plate is blocked in and replaced.

process: Eliminate unnecessary equipment: consolidate storage tanks (PRO 504)
description: Consolidate wellhead crude oil and water storage tanks into one central vessel (and remove oversized or idle equipment) as production declines, cutting standing and working losses.

process: Reduce frequency of replacing modules in turbine meters (PRO 906)
description: Change custody-transfer turbine meter modules every 3 years instead of every 2, avoiding one-sixth of the meter-run blowdowns each year.

The precalciner is a secondary combustion chamber between preheater and rotary kiln where some 65% of total fuel is burnt and 60-65% of total kiln emissions are released; calcination is at least 90% complete before the raw meal reaches the rotary kiln

process: CO2 transport and storage costs (Table 1)

process: Bitumen upgrading to synthetic crude oil (text)

description: Surface mining of oil sand within about 75 m of the surface: oil sand is shovelled by large machines and hauled to an extraction plant, where bitumen is separated from the sand with hot water and chemicals; about 90% of the bitumen is recovered. The bitumen is sold raw or upgraded to synthetic crude oil

process: Cyclic steam stimulation (CSS) thermal in-situ recovery, Canadian oil sands (text)
description: Cyclic steam stimulation: steam is injected into vertical wells to heat the bitumen, which is then pumped to the surface through the same well; recovery about 25-30% of the bitumen. TRAP: the brief writes 'CCS' for cyclic steam stimulation (CSS) throughout the oil-sand text ('two large CCS facilities', 'SOR ... 3.4 for CCS', 'about 70% against 25%-30% from CCS') and misnames it 'Cycle Steam Simulator' - it is NOT carbon capture and storage.

process: SAGD thermal in-situ recovery, Canadian oil sands (text)
description: Steam-assisted gravity drainage: two horizontal wells; steam injected in the upper well heats the bitumen, which drains to and is produced from the lower well. Needs thick, clean deposits; uses less energy and recovers more bitumen (about 70%) than cyclic steam stimulation. Steam raised mostly from natural gas in Canada

process: BGL gasification plants, NETL-401 (Table 1)

process: Chiller

process: Heat pump

Sources include outdoor air, river, lake and sea water, ground heat, industrial and residential waste heat, and sewage heat. In industrial use it replaces boilers in many processes

process: Stationary fuel cell systems

process: Stationary fuel cell systems
detail: electrical efficiency more than 15% below SOFC and MCFC; a candidate for its own archetype

process: Stationary fuel cell systems

process: LanzaTech biomass gasification and fermentation to ethanol, forest residue (Table 1)

state-of-development: As the corn stover case: biomass route at pilot stage (Freedom Pines, expected 2015).

state-of-development: Demonstrated at a 300 t/yr plant with Baosteel (Shanghai) and a second demonstration plant with Shougang (Caofeidian); both exceeded nameplate capacity. Inventory from LanzaTech commercial plant design.

process: Alternative binding materials spotlight (Sect. 4, p.41-45)

process: Alternative binding materials spotlight (Sect. 4, p.41-45)

process: Alternative binding materials spotlight (Sect. 4, p.41-45)

state-of-development: commercial for more than 30 years, mainly in China (about 2 Mt/yr)

process: Alternative binding materials spotlight (Sect. 4, p.41-45)

process: Integrating carbon capture, storage and utilisation (Sect. 4, p.37-40)

state-of-development: pilot at a cement plant in Belgium (LEILAC)

process: Integrating carbon capture, storage and utilisation (Sect. 4, p.37-40)
description: Calcium looping: CO2 separated from flue gas by calcium-oxide sorbents through carbonation-calcination cycles; the purge can replace part of the raw meal.
state-of-development: pilot (1 tCO2/h, Chinese Taipei, 2013); kiln integration studied in Italy

process: Integrating carbon capture, storage and utilisation (Sect. 4, p.37-40)

process: Improving energy efficiency (Sect. 4, p.23-24)

state-of-development: commercial; state-of-the-art, often used in modern plants

process: Alternative binding materials spotlight (Sect. 4, p.41-45)

process: Improving energy efficiency (Sect. 4, p.23-24)

process: Integrating carbon capture, storage and utilisation (Sect. 4, p.37-40)

process: Integrating carbon capture, storage and utilisation (Sect. 4, p.37-40)

state-of-development: not proven at commercial scale; first European demonstration unlikely before 2020

process: Integrating carbon capture, storage and utilisation (Sect. 4, p.37-40)

process: Integrating carbon capture, storage and utilisation (Sect. 4, p.37-40)

process: Excess heat recovery for power generation (Sect. 4, p.36-37)

process: Innovative technology (Sect. 2.3, Tables 4 and 7)

process: Innovative technology (Sect. 2.3, Tables 4 and 7)
description: Finex: fine ore reduced in a series of fluidised-bed reactors by gas from the melter-gasifier, hot-compacted and melted in the melter-gasifier.
state-of-development: industrial innovative technology demonstrated on industrial scale (installed at POSCO, Korea)

process: Innovative technology (Sect. 2.3, Tables 4 and 7)

H2A-Lite pathway: Central ATR w/CCS, NETL 2022 Case 3 basis (ATR+CCS Case 3 sheet)
description: Natural gas is fed into the autothermal reformer (ATR) plant via pipeline at 435 psia, desulfurized, and mixed with steam at 400°C. At these conditions, ethane and heavier species are cracked in a prereformer to avoid subsequent coking in the autothermal reformer reactor. Cryogenic air separation unit provides 95% oxygen feed at 480 psia to the prereformer outlet stream. The autothermal reformer is fed with an overall oxygen to carbon (O₂/C) ratio of 0.65 and a steam to carbon (H₂O/C) ratio of 1.5.

process: H2A-Lite pathway: Central Grid Electrolysis (ALK), 1,035 MW baseline (ALK Electrolyzer Data sheet, 2022$)
description: The modeled system is a standalone grid powered alkaline electrolyzer with a baseline power rating of 1GW. The production system is based on a high-pressure (31 bar cathode) KOH electrolyzer. The H₂ purification subsystem utilizes a deoxidizer to remove O₂ impurity from the H₂ gas stream and a Temperature Swing Adsorption (TSA) subsystem to remove saturated water from the H₂ gas stream. Two TSA adsorption beds are used to provide continuous water removal producing an H₂ product stream with 99.99 mol% H₂ purity.

process: H2A-Lite pathway: Central Grid Electrolysis (PEM), 400 MW baseline (PEM Electrolyzer Data sheet, 2022$)
description: The modeled system is a standalone grid powered PEM electrolyzer with a baseline power rating of 400MW. The production system is based on a generic system using input from several key industry collaborators (KIC) with commercial experience in PEM electrolysis and brief system and subsystem technoeconomic models, the electrolyzer units use process water, passed through deionizing beds, and grid electricity for electrolysis.

process: H2A-Lite pathway: Central Grid Electrolysis (Solid Oxide), 1 GW DC stack input (SOEC Electrolysis Info sheet)
description: The modeled system is a standalone grid powered solid oxide electrolyzer (SOEC) with a baseline electrical power rating of 1GW. Equipment performance and capital cost is estimated via modelling and industry input. To represent a mature commercial technology potential, the underlying production volume assumption is for 1GW per year, which does not exist today.

process: H2A-Lite pathway: Central Methane Pyrolysis (plasma), 187,200 kg/d, PRELIMINARY (Pyrolysis Inputs sheet)
description: Pyrolysis of natural gas is performed in a high temperature (>2000°C) reactor. The reactor gas product is compressed and purified to 99.9% purity H2. Byproducts include carbon nanoparticles suitable for sale as high-value end product feedstock (e.g., carbon black), export steam, and coke.

process: H2A-Lite pathway: Central SMR (no CCS), NETL 2022 Case 1 basis (SMR Case 1 sheet)
description: Natural gas is fed into the steam methane reformer (SMR) plant via a pipeline at 450 psia. The gas is desulfurized, and mixed with steam at 395°C. The reformer reactor is fed with an overall steam to carbon (H₂O/C) ratio of 2.56. The endothermic steam methane reforming reaction is performed on the cold side of a tube-shell heat exchanger and heat is supplied on the hot side of the heat exchanger by combustion of pressure swing adsorber (PSA) effluent and supplemental natural gas.

process: H2A-Lite pathway: Central SMR w/CCS, NETL 2022 Case 2 basis (SMR+CCS Case 2 sheet)
description: Natural gas is fed into the steam methane reformer (SMR) plant via a pipeline at 435 psia. The gas is desulfurized, and mixed with steam at 395°C. The endothermic steam methane reforming reaction is performed on the cold side of a tube-shell heat exchanger and heat is supplied on the hot side of the heat exchanger by combustion of pressure swing adsorber (PSA) effluent and supplemental natural gas.

process: CO2 capture options for lime kilns, numbers from cement studies (Sect. 4.1, Table 3)
description: Calcium looping integrated in the calcination step: CaCO3 carbonation/calcination loop with fresh limestone fed to the combined calciner, extra fuel, oxy-fuel combustion for a pure CO2 stream and a steam cycle on high-grade waste heat

process: CO2 capture options for lime kilns, numbers from cement studies (Sect. 4.1, Table 3)
description: Tail-end calcium looping: kiln flue gas sent to a separate carbonator/calciner loop with a CaO-rich purge returned to the kiln; extra coal, oxy-fuel calciner and steam-cycle power

process: CO2 capture options for lime kilns, numbers from cement studies (Sect. 4.1, Table 3)
description: Hollow-fibre polymeric membrane capture in two stages (1.2 bar then 1.05 bar) followed by CO2 condensation to >99 vol% CO2 at 150 bar; based on the Norcem pilot, applied conceptually to a PFRK

process: CO2 capture options for lime kilns, numbers from cement studies (Sect. 4.1, Table 3)
description: RTI's PEI solid sorption (temperature swing on a supported polyethyleneimine sorbent): Norcem/RTI cement pilot applied conceptually to a PFRK; efficiency drops at higher SOx

process: Lime kiln types, EU-27 (Sect. 2.1, Table 2)
description: Long rotary kiln (LRK): 50-225 m long, 2-6 m diameter rotating cylinder, wet (chain zone) or dry feed, no preheater; flexible and robust, can make lime of varying reactivity from soft stone, but strong convective and radiative losses make it poorly efficient

process: CO2 capture options for lime kilns, numbers from cement studies (Sect. 4.1, Table 3)
description: Oxy-fuel lime kiln: calcination with oxygen from an air separation unit and recycled flue gas, giving a CO2-rich exhaust that a CO2 purification unit cleans and compresses; needs major kiln modification and long shut-downs, with the bulk of the cost in the ASU and CPU

process: Lime kiln types, EU-27 (Sect. 2.1, Table 2)
description: Parallel flow regenerative kiln (PFRK): two shaft kilns, each with preheating, burning and cooling zones, joined by a crossover channel that gives very low specific heat consumption; the most used lime kiln in the EU (158 units in 2013), suitable for different fuels and giving a high-reactivity, low-residual-CO2 quicklime

process: Lime kiln types, EU-27 (Sect. 2.1, Table 2)
description: Long rotary kiln with preheater (PRK): cyclone, shaft or travelling-grate preheaters and often a calciner ahead of a shorter (40-90 m) rotary kiln; better heat recovery, higher maintenance cost and higher electricity use than the LRK

process: Lime kiln types, EU-27 (Sect. 2.1, Table 2)
description: Annular shaft kiln (ASK): central cylinder inside an annular shell with upper and lower burners and heat recovery from the off-gas; medium-high reactivity lime, CO2-rich off-gas (29-34 vol%), longer residence time (8-20 h) and higher construction cost; limestone 40-150 mm

process: Lime kiln types, EU-27 (Sect. 2.1, Table 2)
description: Mixed feed shaft kiln (MFSK): limestone and coke or anthracite fed together down a shaft with preheating and reduction/oxidation burning zones; low electricity use and construction/maintenance cost but sulfur-rich lime of low-to-moderate reactivity

process: Alternative fuels and heat sources for lime kilns (Sect. 4.2)
description: Solar-powered rotary lime kiln (Meier et al.): multi-tube SiC reaction chamber heated by concentrated solar energy; concentrated solar calcination in a long rotary kiln also studied (Abanades)

process: Quicklime slaking (Sect. 3)
description: Hydration of CaO to Ca(OH)2 (dry powder or putty) in slurry, paste, ball-mill or batch slakers, with the exothermic heat (1.14 MJ per kg CaO) recovered to dry the product

process: Calcination-free routes to slaked lime (Sect. 4.3)
description: Electrochemical synthesis of Ca(OH)2 from CaCO3 with simultaneous O2/CO2 and H2 gas production; the process CO2 is released as a concentrated gas that eases capture

process: Calcination-free routes to slaked lime (Sect. 4.3)
description: Room-temperature reaction of CaCO3 with NaOH solution giving Ca(OH)2 and Na2CO3.xH2O (x = 0,1): no combustion, and the process CO2 is locked in the carbonate; laboratory scale

process: Enzymatic PET recycling to rTPA, NREL base case 150 t/d (Tables S1-S4)
description: Enzymatic recycling of PET: clean PET flakes are melt-extruded, quenched and micronised, depolymerised to terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol by a purchased PET hydrolase in stirred-tank reactors (60 degC, pH 8, 96 h, 90% conversion), then rTPA is precipitated with sulfuric acid and crystallised, sodium sulfate crystallised and ethylene glycol distilled (Aspen Plus model).
state-of-development: Conceptual process model (laboratory-scale enzyme performance); no TRL stated

process: Billet reheating (Tables 1-4)
description: hydrogen-fired reheating furnace using electrolytic hydrogen

process: Billet reheating (Tables 1-4)
description: natural gas-fired reheating furnace for steel billets (benchmark)

process: Billet reheating (Tables 1-4)
description: induction reheating of billets with an added static magnetic field

process: Air separation technology comparison (Sect. 2-4, Table 1)
description: Conventional multi-column cryogenic distillation of compressed, pretreated air into oxygen, nitrogen and optionally argon; currently the most efficient and cost-effective route for large quantities.

process: Air separation technology comparison (Sect. 2-4, Table 1)
description: Pressure or vacuum swing adsorption on zeolites that adsorb nitrogen, giving an oxygen-rich stream of typically 93-95 vol%.

process: Air separation technology comparison (Sect. 2-4, Table 1)
description: Chemical air separation (MOLTOX): oxygen absorbed by a circulating molten alkali nitrate/nitrite salt and desorbed by heating and pressure reduction; 99.9% purity at pilot scale, but salt/oxygen corrosion was an economic problem.
state-of-development: developing (pilot unit operated by Air Products)

process: Oxygen supply for a 5000-bpd GTL plant, 890 sTPD at 500 psig (Sect. 6.1)
description: Pressure-swing chemical (molten salt) ASU producing 890 sTPD oxygen at 500 psig, using high-level heat from the partial oxidation process (example estimate).

process: Air separation technology comparison (Sect. 2-4, Table 1)
description: Ion transport membrane: mixed-conducting ceramic oxide operating above 1100 degF that passes oxygen ions under a pressure difference, suited to integration with gas turbines and partial oxidation.
state-of-development: developing (embryonic); best candidate to challenge cryogenics for high-purity tonnage oxygen

process: Air separation technology comparison (Sect. 2-4, Table 1)
description: Polymeric membranes permeating oxygen faster than nitrogen, giving oxygen-enriched air (25-50% oxygen) at near-ambient conditions with a blower and vacuum pump.

process: Oxygen supply for a 5000-bpd GTL plant, 890 sTPD at 500 psig (Sect. 6.1)
description: Full pumped liquid oxygen cryogenic cycle producing 890 sTPD of oxygen at 500 psig for a 5000-bpd gas-to-liquids plant (example estimate).

process: Ammonia synthesis
description: medium-pressure (20 bar) Haber-Bosch loop with ammonia separated by absorption in metal halides (MgCl2 or CaCl2) instead of condensation

process: Ammonia synthesis
description: electrically driven Haber-Bosch: alkaline or PEM electrolysis, PSA nitrogen, electric compressors, 150 bar loop

process: Ammonia synthesis
description: low-pressure (3 bar) Haber-Bosch with in situ ammonia absorption in the reactor (250-300 degC)

process: Ammonia synthesis
description: methane-fed Haber-Bosch ammonia plant (best available technique)

process: Zinc plant modernization and expansion, Flin Flon MB (HBM&S project sheet)
description: Replacement of the 1930s electrolytic tankhouse at the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting zinc plant by a modern-technology tankhouse (Asturiana de Zinc technology, Spain) making SHG zinc cathodes, with changes to the zinc pressure leach, purification and casting sections
state-of-development: commercial: new tankhouse completed 2001 at an operating plant that has run since 1930

process: Chemical recycling of household plastic waste (Sect. 3-4, Table 3)
description: Conventional gasification of plastic waste with air, oxygen-enriched air, oxygen or steam to syngas; e.g. Enerkem Edmonton steam gasification of 100,000 t/y sorted waste to methanol and ethanol.

process: Chemical recycling of household plastic waste (Sect. 3-4, Table 3)
description: Plasma gasification: plasma torches heat air to create plasma that converts organic matter to syngas and inorganic matter to inert slag; very high electricity requirement.

process: Chemical recycling of household plastic waste (Sect. 3-4, Table 3)
description: Hydrocracking: low-temperature pyrolysis liquefaction followed by cracking over a catalyst bed under hydrogen at about 70 atm; cannot treat PVC; pilot scale for waste plastics.

process: Chemical recycling of household plastic waste (Sect. 3-4, Table 3)
description: Conventional pyrolysis (thermal cracking): plastics cracked at moderate to high temperature in the absence of oxygen to gas, char and pyrolysis oil, which often needs upgrading; low tolerance to PVC.

process: Chemical recycling of household plastic waste (Sect. 3-4, Table 3)
description: Catalytic cracking: pyrolysis with a catalyst that lowers the process temperature and raises the oil yield; sensitive to chloride, nitrogen and inorganic contaminants.

process: Chemical recycling of household plastic waste (Sect. 3-4, Table 3)
description: Pyrolysis with in-line reforming: two connected reactors, pyrolysis then catalytic steam reforming of the volatiles to a tar-free, hydrogen-rich gas (usually over 30% hydrogen).

process: Chemical recycling of household plastic waste (Sect. 3-4, Table 3)
description: Microwave-assisted pyrolysis: plastics mixed with a dielectric absorbent heated by microwaves; studied at laboratory and pilot scale (e.g. Stena Metall 2003-2005).

process: Chemical recycling of household plastic waste (Sect. 3-4, Table 3)
description: Plasma pyrolysis: conventional pyrolysis integrated with thermal plasma, decomposing waste plastics to syngas (mainly CO and H2) in 0.01-0.5 s.

process: Hot gas generators for directly heated dryers (Sect. 2.6)

process: MDF fibre drying, per tonne dry fibre (Sect. 3.1.4, Table 3.3)
description: Fibres leaving the refiner pass through a 20-30 m blowline where resin is added, then dry in directly heated tube dryers of 150-180 m length (some indirectly heated by steam coils), residence time 3-10 s.

process: MDF fibre drying (Sect. 3.1.4, Table 3.2)
description: Fibres leaving the refiner pass through a 20-30 m blowline where resin is added, then dry in directly heated tube dryers of 150-180 m length (some indirectly heated by steam coils), residence time 3-10 s.

process: Particleboard drying, indirectly heated dryers (Sect. 3.1.4, Table 3.2 footnotes)
description: Indirectly heated rotary dryer in which wood particles are heated by radiation heat from steam coils supplied by on-site boilers or gas engines, often combined with a CHP plant; recirculation or added hot gas gives combination dryers.

process: Superheated steam dryers, emerging (Sect. 6.1)
description: Dryer using superheated steam where the excess energy in steam evaporated from the wood could be used for power generation or heat exchange; applied in other sectors and for drying wood pellets or fibres.
state-of-development: Emerging technique; energy-saving potential not yet developed in the wood-based panel sector.

process: OSB strand drying (Sect. 3.1.4, Table 3.2)
description: Rotary bundle, drum or tubular dryers drying chips, flakes or strands with hot gas from on-site combustion plants (directly heated) or by radiation heat from steam coils (indirectly heated); the most energy-intensive step in panel production. OSB strands are dried to 5-10 % moisture for pMDI resin; no indirectly heated OSB dryers are reported (Table 3.5).

process: Particleboard drying (Sect. 3.1.4, Table 3.2)
description: Rotary bundle, drum or tubular dryers drying chips, flakes or strands with hot gas from on-site combustion plants (directly heated) or by radiation heat from steam coils (indirectly heated); the most energy-intensive step in panel production.

process: UTWS combined heat and dryer system, plant D012 particleboard (Sect. 4.2.2.3, Table 4.2)
description: Combined heat and dryer system (UTWS): dryer waste gas is reheated in a heat exchanger fed by combustion flue-gas and returned to the dryer; part is post-combusted; closed loop with no dryer stack; combustion plant fires a mix of wood and natural gas.
state-of-development: Developed in Europe around 2000; installed at four installations in Europe.

process: UTWS combined heat and dryer system, plant D096 OSB (Sect. 4.2.2.3, Table 4.2)
description: Combined heat and dryer system (UTWS): dryer waste gas is reheated in a heat exchanger fed by combustion flue-gas and returned to the dryer; part is post-combusted; closed loop with no dryer stack; combustion plant fires a mix of wood and natural gas.
state-of-development: Developed in Europe around 2000; installed at four installations in Europe.

process: MDF pressing (Sect. 3.1.4, Table 3.2)
description: Continuous (20-60 m) or multi-opening press compressing the resinated mat at high pressure, with press belts or plates heated by thermal oil (contact temperature normally not above 260 degC) to cure the resin.

process: OSB pressing (Sect. 3.1.4, Table 3.2)
description: Continuous (20-60 m) or multi-opening press compressing the resinated mat at high pressure, with press belts or plates heated by thermal oil (contact temperature normally not above 260 degC) to cure the resin.

process: Particleboard pressing (Sect. 3.1.4, Table 3.2)
description: Continuous (20-60 m) or multi-opening press compressing the resinated mat at high pressure, with press belts or plates heated by thermal oil (contact temperature normally not above 260 degC) to cure the resin.

process: MDF fibre refining and drying combined (Sect. 3.1.4, Table 3.3)

process: MDF fibre refining, per tonne dry fibre (Sect. 3.1.4, Table 3.3)
description: Wood chips are pre-cooked, steam-cooked under pressure and defibrated between refiner discs (similar to thermo-mechanical pulping); fibres are blown directly into the blowline and dryer.

process: MDF fibre refining (Sect. 3.1.4, Table 3.2)

process: Thermal-oil heating for presses (Sect. 2.6)

process: Biomass-fired CHP plant for indirect drying (Sect. 4.6.4)
