process: Glass melting furnace types (Sect. 3.2.1, Table 6, Table B2)
description: Hybrid melter or electric boosting: fuel firing (natural gas or hydrogen) combined with submerged electrodes, with electric energy shares up to 80% in the first commercial hybrid melters (pull up to 400 t/d), giving longer lifetime, higher cullet share and pull flexibility than all-electric furnaces

process: Glass melting furnace types (Sect. 3.2.1, Table 6, Table B2)
description: Oxy-fuel glass melting furnace: fuel burned with oxygen of more than 92 vol% purity, no heat recovery, lower flue-gas volume (mostly CO2 and water), NOx cut 70-90%; mainly used in special glass for process and quality reasons rather than economics

process: Glass melting furnace types (Sect. 3.2.1, Table 6, Table B2)
description: Recuperative glass melting furnace: tube-bundle steel recuperators continuously preheat combustion air to at most 700-800 degC, separated from the flue gas; smaller capacity, cleaner and more stable combustion than regenerative, with efficiency falling less at low throughput

process: Glass melting furnace types (Sect. 3.2.1, Table 6, Table B2)
description: Regenerative end-port (end-fired) glass melting furnace: burners at the charging end firing parallel to the melt flow, two alternately operated regenerators preheating combustion air to about 1300 degC or more; about 75% of global container glass companies use it

process: Glass melting furnace types (Sect. 3.2.1, Table 6, Table B2)
description: Regenerative side-port (cross-fired) glass melting furnace with 5-8 regenerators on each side; almost 90% of flat glass furnaces worldwide, including the float glass furnace; larger melting capacity than end-port

process: Glass melting furnace types (Sect. 3.2.1, Table 6, Table B2)
description: Glass furnace fired on hydrogen (co-firing or 100%): higher flame temperature, changed flame length and heat transfer, more water vapour in the flue gas, higher NOx (oxy-fuel can compensate); burner and infrastructure modifications needed; hydrogen-oxy-fuel viable if oxygen prices fall

process: Waste heat recovery to the furnace (Sect. 4.1, Tables 7-8, 11)
description: Thermochemical heat recovery (TCR) on oxy-fuel furnaces: natural gas mixed with about 20% recirculated hot flue gas is steam-reformed in regenerator checkers to a hot syngas that burns with oxygen; recovers about 60% of the flue-gas sensible heat; regenerator volume only about 33% of an air-regenerative furnace

process: Heat-to-power from furnace waste heat (Sect. 4.1.4, Table 9)
description: Thermoelectric generator on flue gas: no moving parts, very low maintenance, start-up in seconds, water cooling needed; low efficiency

process: Glass melting furnace types (Sect. 3.2.1, Table 6, Table B2)
description: All-electric glass melting furnace (cold-top, submerged electrodes, Joule heating in the melt): about 85% thermal efficiency, smaller furnace volume, no regenerators or high-temperature crown, no carry-over; limited capacity, pull window of 80-110% of nominal, shorter lifetime, not suitable for every glass type

process: Model assumptions for electric melting and hydrogen firing (Sect. 6, Table B2)
Glass melting furnace types (Sect. 3.2.1, Table 6, Table B2)
description: Microwave glass melting: fast and efficient but standing waves, glass transparent to microwaves below 300 degC and scale-up challenges

process: Glass melting furnace types (Sect. 3.2.1, Table 6, Table B2)
description: Plasma glass melting with a DC torch (argon) on a rotating skull; very short residence time (5-15 min) but scale-up, argon cost and low TRL block industrial use

process: Waste heat recovery to the furnace (Sect. 4.1, Tables 7-8, 11)
description: Batch and cullet preheating (indirect Zippe, Linde, TNO; direct Nienburger): exhaust heat warms batch and cullets before charging; batch preheating risks clogging so it needs high cullet shares or pelletised batch

process: Waste heat recovery to the furnace (Sect. 4.1, Tables 7-8, 11)
description: Direct cullet preheating (e.g. Sorg): exhaust gas at about 500 degC enters the cullet preheater and leaves at about 200 degC, cullets typically preheated to about 400 degC; sensible for high cullet shares (container glass)

process: Heat-to-power from furnace waste heat (Sect. 4.1.4, Table 9)
description: Steam Rankine cycle on furnace exhaust: higher efficiency but very high maintenance and long start-up; auxiliaries are piping, steam generator, desalination plant, feed-water tank

process: Heat-to-power from furnace waste heat (Sect. 4.1.4, Table 9)
description: Organic Rankine cycle on furnace exhaust: low maintenance, dynamic operation, start-up in minutes; best available heat-to-power option in the glass industry; auxiliaries are piping and heat exchanger

process: Hybrid electric plus hydrogen option, warm-top melter (Table 1, App. G)

process: Thermo-chemical heat recovery option (Table 1, App. F)
description: Oxy-fuel combustion combined with heat recovery: natural gas is blended with about 20% recirculated hot flue gas (H2O, CO2) to reform it to a hot synthesis gas of mainly H2 and CO with higher LHV; assumed on a regenerative furnace.
